sections.h2: How is an Indiana property tax bill calculated?
sections.html:
An Indiana bill starts with gross assessed value, subtracts deductions to reach net assessed value, multiplies by the local rate, and then applies credits and a cap. The Department of Local Government Finance (DLGF) walks through the sequence in its Tax Bill 101 page.

  • Deductions such as the homestead and mortgage deductions come off first.
  • Every property in the same taxing district pays the same local rate, built from county, city, school, township and library levies.
  • Percentage credits come next, some of them funded by local option income tax revenue.
  • A circuit breaker credit then pulls the bill down to the cap if it is still too high.
  • Special assessments, such as ditch charges, are added at the end.

The cap does not touch the local rate. Budgets set that, and the cap only limits what a given owner pays against the property's gross assessed value.

sections.h2: What are the Indiana property tax caps?
sections.html:
Indiana limits the tax on a home to 1 percent of its gross assessed value, and other property classes have higher limits. Voters put the caps into Article 10, Section 1 of the state constitution in November 2010, and they have applied since the 2010 tax bills.

Property classCap on gross assessed value
Homestead (must receive the standard deduction)1%
Other residential, long-term care, agricultural land2%
Nonresidential and personal property3%

The fact sheet gives a simple example. A $100,000 homestead with a $2,100 liability gets a $1,100 credit and ends up at the $1,000 cap. Most counties exclude certain voter-approved school and public safety levies and some capital project levies from the cap, which is why a statement can show an adjustment to the cap amount. Beginning with Pay 2025, residential yard structures count as residential property under the 2 percent cap.

Apartments, vacation homes and other non-homestead residential property sit under the 2 percent cap, which matters for heirs who keep an inherited house as a rental.

sections.h2: When are Indiana property taxes due, and what does a late payment cost?
sections.html:
Under IC 6-1.1-22-9, the tax for a year is paid in two equal installments the following year, due May 10 and November 10. A bill for 2025 property is therefore a 2026 payment, which is why DLGF labels it "2025 Pay 2026." A due date that lands on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day, so the 2026 spring installment was due May 11.

The penalty depends on timing. A payment made within 30 days after the due date, by an owner with no earlier delinquency on the parcel, carries a 5 percent penalty. Otherwise the penalty is 10 percent. In later years, an extra 10 percent is added to unpaid principal on the day after each installment date.

A few details help at closing:

  • A county council can require taxes under $25 to be paid in one May installment.
  • If an appeal changes levies, a reconciling statement shows any remaining balance, payable by November 10 unless the county sets other dates.

Because Indiana bills a year behind, the title company works out the tax proration at closing.

sections.h2: How did Indiana's 2025 law change the homestead deduction?
sections.html:
Senate Enrolled Act 1 of 2025 is phasing out the flat homestead standard deduction and replacing part of it with a percentage deduction. DLGF's 2026 memo on deductions and credits lays out the schedule.

YearStandard deduction (assessment date)Supplemental deduction percentage (taxes payable)
2025$48,000not listed in the memo
2026$40,00040%
2027$30,00046%
2028$20,00052%
2029$10,00057%
2030$062%
2031 and later$066.7%

An Indiana Fiscal Policy Institute analysis from November 2025 estimates that owners of lower-value homes may see double-digit increases, while owners of expensive homes may see small decreases. It puts the breakeven between the two deductions at a $102,740 home. It also describes a new 10 percent supplemental credit, up to $300, that applies after the caps starting in 2026.

Other changes matter for sellers and heirs. Over 65 relief became a credit instead of a deduction, and from January 1, 2026 the claimant must live on the property. Veterans with a service-connected disability of at least 10 percent can claim a $350 credit, and veterans at least 62 with a 10 percent disability can claim a $250 credit. From July 1, 2026, an owner who keeps a homestead deduction after becoming ineligible owes back taxes plus a 10 percent civil penalty. That is a point to check when a house sits empty after an owner moves to care or passes away.

sections.h2: How are Indiana assessments set and adjusted?
sections.html:
Assessing officials adjust real property values every year, using mass appraisal methods that follow DLGF rules, and they must notify the owner when an adjustment raises the assessment. IC 6-1.1-4-4.5 sets that framework for the years between general reassessments, and the adjustments are tied to estimated true tax value as of the assessment date that sets the taxes payable.

The Form 11 notice of assessment is the paper that starts the appeal clock, and the appeal path runs from Form 130 through the county assessment board to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131. The summary above gives the deadlines. The sales disclosure form filed at closing feeds transfer prices to the state and county, which use them in yearly adjustments.

sections.h2: What happens when Indiana property taxes go unpaid?
sections.html:
Unpaid taxes can put a parcel on the county's tax sale list, and a buyer at that sale gets a certificate rather than the house. Under IC 6-1.1-24-1, real property is eligible when taxes from the prior year's spring installment or earlier are delinquent and the amount owed, with penalties and fees, is more than $25. The county treasurer certifies the list after January 1 of the sale year and within 51 days after the first payment due date.

A parcel cannot sell for less than a minimum bid made up of the following:

  • delinquent taxes and special assessments;
  • taxes and assessments due in the sale year, even if not yet delinquent;
  • penalties on those delinquencies;
  • the county's sale costs and any unpaid costs from a prior sale;
  • other reasonable collection costs, including title search and attorney's fees.

Property on a county's vacant and abandoned list can sell for less and carries no right of redemption after the sale.

Everyone else keeps a redemption window. IC 6-1.1-25-4 sets it at one year after the sale, or 120 days when the buyer is a qualified purchasing agency. Redemption costs 110 percent of the minimum bid within six months of the sale, or 115 percent after six months, plus interest on any excess bid, taxes the buyer paid, and certified costs. The county treasurer and the owner may agree to a payment arrangement that extends the period, generally to one year after the agreement.

sections.h2: Can an owner sell a house after a tax sale or with tax due?
sections.html:
An owner can sell with taxes due, because the payoff is settled at closing, but a sale during the redemption period has extra steps. Under IC 32-21-8-7, the county auditor cannot endorse the conveyance until the buyer pays the county treasurer the full redemption amount and gives the auditor written proof. The deed is then void unless it is recorded by the end of the redemption period.

When a tax sale buyer's purchase is not redeemed, the former owner can still file a verified claim for money in the tax sale surplus fund, and the surplus not claimed within three years of receipt moves to the county general fund.

sections.h2: What do Indiana sellers see on their tax statement in 2026?
sections.html:
The 2026 statement adds credit lines for the Over 65 Credit, the Blind/Disabled Credit, the Supplemental Homestead Credit and the County Option Homestead Relief Credit. DLGF's memo on the 2026 TS-1 also splits each tax rate into debt and non-debt parts and adds a percentage of total liability column.

Every taxpayer gets a bill, even with a zero balance, and escrowed accounts may carry an "In Escrow" or "For Informational Purposes Only" watermark.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Indiana?
faqs.a: They are due in two equal installments, May 10 and November 10 of the year after the assessment year. When the date falls on a weekend or holiday the deadline moves to the next business day, which is why the 2026 spring installment was due May 11.

faqs.q: What is the Indiana property tax cap for a home?
faqs.a: The cap is 1 percent of gross assessed value for a homestead that receives the standard deduction. Other residential property and agricultural land are capped at 2 percent, and nonresidential and personal property at 3 percent.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for paying Indiana property tax late?
faqs.a: A 5 percent penalty applies to a payment made within 30 days after the due date if the parcel has no earlier delinquency. Otherwise the penalty is 10 percent, and an extra 10 percent can be added to unpaid tax in later years.

faqs.q: How long do I have to redeem property after an Indiana tax sale?
faqs.a: The period is one year after the sale, or 120 days when the buyer is a qualified purchasing agency. Redemption costs 110 percent of the minimum bid within six months and 115 percent after that, plus the other statutory amounts. Vacant and abandoned property has no redemption right.

faqs.q: Is the Indiana homestead deduction going away?
faqs.a: The flat standard deduction drops from $48,000 for 2025 to $40,000 for 2026 and reaches $0 in 2030, while the supplemental percentage deduction rises toward 66.7 percent by 2031. Owners must keep reporting if they stop living in the home.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house that has back property taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. Back taxes and penalties are paid from closing proceeds, and the title company can request the payoff figure from the county treasurer. If the parcel has already been sold at a tax sale, the redemption amount must be paid before the auditor will endorse the deed.
